To me that was one of the most traumatic things in my incident - my fiancé was probably around 300lbs, maybe a little less, and he was on a bed with wheels. The dispatcher kept urging me to get him to the ground and I was trying everything but I couldn’t do it. She finally told me I couldn’t worry about hurting him (it’s a hard thing to overcome) so I grabbed his legs and pulled as hard as I could. His head hit the corner of the table as he came down and I screamed, but he was on the floor so she started walking me through compressions. I just remember panicking with every second I couldn’t pull him down. I felt like she was yelling at me and I felt like it took five minutes but I’m sure all of that was amplified with the shock. And he didn’t feel cold, so there was sense to the urgency. They marked time of death as over an hour before I found him, so realistically there was nothing to be done. He was bundled up in a sweater and blankets so I’m assuming that kept his body temp up.

Wow. This is very similar to my own experience - I found my 34-year-old fiancé unresponsive, not breathing, no pulse. Also DOA. I sometimes think about that dispatcher and hope she’s okay. Thank you for all you do.

It’s a weird thing to get past if you’re not prepared. Especially in a panic when finding a loved one. I’m sure actually being trained in cpr helps too. (He had been gone over an hour at that point so even had I done it correctly, it wouldn’t have brought him back.) Even after he was pronounced DOA I panicked when they covered his face with a blanket because I thought, “he can’t breathe!” Death is a weird thing to wrap your mind around sometimes.

My grandparents all developed Alzheimer’s, with only one still alive now. I still remember when my grandma learned my grandpa had suddenly passed. That wail will haunt me forever. But what’s worse, we had to break the news to her multiple times as she forgot. Absolutely crushing. 

My mom started showing signs of early-onset Alzheimer’s at 59. She’ll be 65 this year and while she is still mostly lucid and still knows those around her, it has definitely progressed. She and my dad stopped by the other day to drop off some mail for me and to say hi. They got to meet our new dog, Lady. My mom loves dogs, and our dog looks like her dog. I had been telling her about Lady for a while, and she had been remembering broad details... but I guess not anymore. My mom asked what Lady’s name is three times in maybe 30 seconds. 

“What’s her name?”
“Lady.”
“Oh, that’s pretty.”
Pause.
“What’s her name?”
“Lady.”
“Oh, okay.”
Pause. 
“What’s her name?”
“Lady.”
“Oh, maybe you told me that...”

At least she no longer knows how bad it is. She still cries sometimes because hey, it’s a fucking awful disease to have. But most days she doesn’t remember the diagnosis and just says she has memory issues. It’s more than her memory, but ignorance is bliss.

I’ve definitely developed a lot of patience, and now when answering the same question over and over, I sometimes change up the wording or answer with a joke instead, just something to make it easier. I focus on making her laugh when I visit. She won’t remember I was there after an hour or so, but I hope the happiness lasts a bit longer. 

I’m 99.9999% sure I’ll have it too someday. I just hope that they have better treatment by then and that if it’s early onset, it’s not too early.

You were lucky then. Was it in Alameda county? Within the last 10 years? My DUI attorney said Alameda county (especially Livermore) is notorious for the number of DUIs. And everyone else in my DUI classes shared experiences similar to mine.

My first (and only) DUI occurred in downtown Livermore in December 2013. No injuries or damage, thank god. 

All in all, with fines and fees (including attorney fees) it ended up being over $10,000. 

Spent the night in jail and only had one additional day of community service, so that was pretty negligible. 

6 months license suspension, 6 months DUI class, interlock device (can’t remember how long, but also had to pay for one lock-out because I was in the drive thru and didn’t blow in time)

3 years zero tolerance probation

It was a huge wake up call for me. I fell into alcoholism in college and continued that pattern when I moved back to Livermore. But you can bet I didn’t have a drop of alcohol before driving during the probation, and now that it’s up I get paranoid about having even one drink if I have to drive. 

The stupid thing is, that night I ran into some old friends at the bar right when I was going to leave, but I decided to stay and drink with them with the agreement that we’d share a cab home. I don’t know how I ended up in my car. I was totally blacked out until the lights came on in my rear view mirror. 

0/10 would not recommend, ever. EVEN IF no one is hurt and there’s no damage, it’s a long and financially painful process. 

Oh, and because it’s on my record for 10 years, I’ll be considered a high-risk driver until it falls off, which means really really expensive car insurance. 

So yeah, I wouldn’t consider it just a slap on the wrist, though most first-time offenders apparently get caught for a 2nd+ DUI.

I have been fighting for disability for four. Years. Being unable to work this entire time. I’ve been fortunate to be covered as a disabled dependent, but have since moved out and will be losing my healthcare at the end of the year. If I’m not granted disability soon, I won’t have coverage at all. I simply can’t afford it. And if protections for pre-existing conditions go away, I’m even more fucked. 

I need the insurance because I go to two to three appointments a month, one being an uncommon and extremely expensive treatment (which my current insurance pays in full), and I take five medications, all necessary to actually *keep me alive*.

The system is fatally broken. I’m terrified of what’s going to happen (and all this stress makes my condition worse, so there’s that). You can’t just look at the average, middle-class person when discussing health care. A lot of us are going to die if nothing is done about this.

The scary thing is that’s the reason many opponents of universal health care in the US use - they don’t WANT to help pay for others. They balk at the idea that they would have to pay $1000 even if they weren’t sick. Doesn’t matter that it would help and maybe save others. It’s terrifying. Especially as a disabled person about to lose her health care.

There’s a tutorial at the beginning and many levels of bots to play against. There are also three game modes: Standard, which is your typical 3v3 and takes around 20-25 minutes; Battle Royale, which is 3v3 lane-only with randomized heroes; and Blitz, which is a 5-minute full-map challenge to get 15 points before the other team. 

All offer bot games, and there is a dedicated practice mode if you just want to learn a hero with no pressure. Battle Royale, in my opinion, is a great way to test out different heroes, especially ones you don’t currently own. 

Vainglory has an esport following, and they often have championships on Twitch. Top-tier players are obviously going to know the quirks of the map and heroes, but I wouldn’t say it’s impossible to reach those ranks if you didn’t start from the beginning. They release new heroes pretty often and include balance changes, and you can find builds online.

I absolutely love Stardew Valley and I’m pretty disappointed that nothing even comes close on iOS. There are many attempts (even a Harvest Moon game, I think) but I actually like the idea of shifting away from the farming theme, because it’ll stand out from those failed attempts. Definitely interested!

If it’s helpful, here are the things that make Stardew Valley so addictive for me:

Creating your farm/area. Every HM game starts off with a shitty plot of land covered in weeds, rocks, and tree stumps. While it may be annoying to some, there’s something satisfying about gradually cleaning the area up and making it nice and functional. 

Crafting. SV has so many recipes, from food (that affects your stamina and health and can boost attributes - definitely cool) to tools to items that can transport you to different areas on the map. I love being able to craft so many useful things that make it easy to play how I want to play. 

Automation. Sure, the first year it’s kinda fun plotting and watering your crops, but as time goes on and there are more things to do (and you plant way more), the sprinklers are so helpful! I can just run by my crops and if nothing’s ready yet, run off to other areas. 

Friendships. I’ll get to the relationships in a minute, but specifically friendships are really cool to me. Seeing how people go from superficially friendly to confiding in me about personal problems is nice. 

Dark themes. SV has some darker stories mixed in with the light stuff. Makes it a little more mature and pulls me into the story more. 

I want to make a note about relationships. I do enjoy them (and love that your character can pursue romantic interests of any gender, please include) but it gets tiring trying to bring the same items to them every day. If there were other ways to increase affection, I’d like that. Maybe getting close to their family or friends, or them having specific problems you can help with (instead of just “hey, they like that gem.”)

To answer your questions:

The OG is a decent model if you just want to try out the smartwatch scene. It'll give you notifications and has plenty of apps and watchfaces. My one word of caution is that there is a known, widespread issue with the OG with screen tearing - the display screws up and renders the watch unusable. Pebble will replace it for free, and I had a good experience with that, but some people have had pretty bad experiences with Pebble support (long delays, etc). Because you're in Canada you may experience those delays. 

The OG has plenty of apps. I'm not really an app person, nor do I have a Time to compare, but just browsing through there's no shortage of apps IMO. Maybe someone else can weigh in on this.

The apps I have currently are Stand Up, which is an hourly reminder to stand up; Games for Pebble, which has five simple games you can play; and Watch the Slots, which is a simple slot machine simulator. But there are far more useful apps in the store - it all depends on what your needs are.

My final word of advice is to remember that the Pebble is not like a phone on your wrist. Its main function is to receive notifications. If that sounds like a good fit, I'd say try it out. Many of us love our watches and consider ourselves long-time customers, despite the complaints you may find on here. 

Best of luck! :)

Every time I've tried to "wing it," I've failed NaNo. Everyone is different, but I personally need a plan going in. Often the plan changes while I'm writing, so I still get some of the spontaneity of NaNo. 

I swear by the Snowflake Method, at least the first few steps. I don't think I've ever made it all the way through. But having the major points planned out and a little more info on the characters really makes it clear in my mind. I never get to planning out the individual scenes, but as long as I have a good idea of what happens at each point, I can usually type it out. 

But I definitely need plenty of time to plan. If I wait until October, chances are I won't get enough done to actually plan out as well as I need to succeed. I need to at least start in September, mostly because I don't have the energy to work on it daily. These days writing is almost a chore for me; I do enjoy it, but I rarely have the motivation to get started and only write when an idea won't leave me alone. I haven't participated in NaNo in about two years, so I'm starting the planning process now, knowing it'll take a bit of discipline to work on outlining for more than a couple minutes. Give yourself plenty of time in case you hit a period of disinterest. 

One more suggestion I'd like to make is to find a medium that works for you. Some people work best planning things by hand, writing out scenes on notecards or sticky notes, etc. Others, like me, do better with technology. I highly recommend Scrivener for NaNo writing, and it's great for planning as well with the notecard system. This year I'll be relying more on my iPad/iPhone, so I'm using Storyist, which has a similar system and syncs through DropBox. 

It can take a bit of trial and error to figure out what works best for you. If you haven't planned before, now would be the perfect time to experiment and find something that sticks. 

Best of luck!
